reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant tumour syndrome caused by inactivating mutations in the MEN1 gene encoding menin
Classically involves the three P organs: parathyroid glands, pancreatic islets and enteroendocrine cells, and the anterior pituitary
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common and usually earliest manifestation, typically from multigland parathyroid hyperplasia
Pancreatic and duodenal neuroendocrine tumours include gastrinomas, which can cause Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and insulinomas
Pituitary adenomas, most often prolactinomas, complete the classic triad
Other associated lesions include foregut carcinoids, adrenal cortical tumours and cutaneous features such as angiofibromas and collagenomas
Gene carriers require lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance to detect tumours early
reference.pathophysiology: MEN1 encodes menin, a nuclear protein acting as a tumour suppressor involved in transcriptional regulation and genome stability. Affected individuals inherit one defective allele, and tumours arise when the remaining functional allele is lost within an endocrine cell, consistent with a two-hit mechanism. Loss of menin function removes a brake on proliferation in susceptible endocrine tissues, giving rise to hyperplasia and multiple, often synchronous or metachronous, neoplasms across the parathyroids, pancreatic islets and pituitary. The multiglandular and recurrent nature of disease reflects this germline predisposition throughout the endocrine system.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary endocrine tumour syndromes such as MEN4 or hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone to detect primary hyperparathyroidism
Gut hormone profile including fasting gastrin and other pancreatic peptides
Prolactin and anterior pituitary hormone assessment
Cross-sectional and functional imaging of the pancreas and pituitary for tumour surveillance
Molecular genetic testing of MEN1 for the index case and at-risk relatives
redFlags: Severe hypercalcaemia or peptic ulceration and diarrhoea suggesting a functioning gastrinoma
Rapidly enlarging or metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour
Visual field loss or hormone excess from an expanding pituitary adenoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends largely on pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, which are the leading disease-related cause of death, so structured lifelong surveillance and timely intervention are central to improving long-term outcomes.
pitfalls: Treating hyperparathyroidism as single-gland disease and overlooking multigland involvement
Failing to screen for MEN1 in a young patient with primary hyperparathyroidism or multiple endocrine tumours
Not offering genetic testing and surveillance to at-risk family members
Attributing peptic ulcer disease to common causes and missing an underlying gastrinoma
management: Subtotal or total parathyroidectomy for the multigland primary hyperparathyroidism, with cinacalcet where surgery is unsuitable

Proton-pump inhibitors to control gastrinoma-related Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, with surgical resection of insulinomas and larger pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and somatostatin analogues where appropriate
Dopamine agonists for prolactinoma and trans-sphenoidal surgery for other functioning or compressive pituitary adenomas
Structured lifelong biochemical and cross-sectional and functional imaging surveillance, since pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are the leading cause of disease-related death
Molecular MEN1 testing of the index case with cascade screening of at-risk relatives
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant syndrome
